qa.recommendation: Keep 104 MW for unit CT4. No change needed. The federal EIA generator table gives 104 MW as the nameplate rating and 72 MW as the summer and winter rating. The 75 MW in the Board of Public Utilities testimony is most likely an operating or net figure, not the nameplate. GEM records nameplate, so 104 MW stands.
qa.note: I compared the sources for this unit. The EIA table for August 2026 lists plant 6064, generator CT4, a natural gas combustion turbine that started in 2006, with nameplate 104 MW and summer and winter capability of 72 MW. The EIA annual survey file for 2024 shows the same three numbers. The Board of Public Utilities testimony from a 2023 rate hearing, by its executive director of electric production, calls CT4 the newest 75 MW oil and gas unit. That testimony does not say whether 75 MW is nameplate, net or summer. It also calls the coal unit 245 Net MW while EIA lists that unit at 261 MW nameplate and 243 MW net, so the testimony appears to use net or operating figures. A 75 MW figure sits close to the 72 MW EIA net rating and well below the 104 MW nameplate, which fits that pattern. A third source, a federal air-data map site, lists a generator 4 at 94 MW, which is probably an older EIA entry and does not match any current rating. I searched for a Board resource plan, annual report, rate filing, Kansas air permit and Southwest Power Pool document that gives the turbine model or a nameplate rating. The Kansas air permit pages did not open and no other document gave a turbine model or a different nameplate. The testimony PDF is gone from the Board's site, but a saved copy from January 2025 still has the 75 MW sentence. I read the EIA annual 2024 file from a local copy; the verifier could not read the zip file.
